title: Paul's defenses and gains are proved fruitful by the Philippians; 'as' means intensity; former gains counted loss only by comparison; refuse is part of the stalk
english: For whether I make my defense when I am accused for the sake of those who believe, and you are among them, or whether I want to confirm the gospel for some, I do it from your steadfastness. And when I want to show that my chains are not without profit, I prove it from your faith.

Paul says, “And being found in form as a man” (Philippians 2:7). The word “as” does not express likeness but intensity. It is like the phrase “as God is good to Israel” (Psalm 73:1, LXX 72:1), and “as I have loved your law, O Lord” (Psalm 119:97, LXX 118:97), meaning “I have loved it very much.”

When Paul says, “holding fast to the word of life” (Philippians 2:16), he means “paying attention to the word of life.” To Timothy he also writes, “Pay attention to yourself” (1 Timothy 4:16), meaning “attend to yourself.”

If Paul considers these things loss for the sake of Christ, they were not bad things; they were gains. And he said “I have considered.” For they were not loss, but by comparison with the surpassing greatness of better things he considers them loss.
The refuse is part of the stalk, and the stalk and the ear of grain once came from the seed.

orientation: Oecumenius is explaining Paul's words in Philippians, showing that Paul's defenses, gospel-confirmation, and endurance of bonds are all proved fruitful by the Philippians' faith and steadfastness, then glossing the force of 'as' and the comparison by which former gains are counted loss.

title: The refuse was once useful for the seed to grow
english: So this refuse was once most useful for the seed to be produced. For just as root, stalk, and ear of grain come from a seed, so from the faith of Abraham, as from a seed, came the root from those in the law, and the stalk of the prophets and the ear of grain already proclaiming Christ in secret. Their harvest and threshing took place at the first coming of the Savior, whose winnowing fork is in his hand and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor.

baehrens: PG 118-119; Fragmenta in epistulam ad Philippenses (Khazarzar) u01 rem mid
orientation: Oecumenius is explaining Paul's word 'refuse' by comparing the law and prophets to a stalk that grew from the seed of Abraham's faith.

title: The law as refuse and the forward-looking mind
english: So then the stalk of the law ceased, and circumcision, Sabbath-keeping, and the other things were separated off like refuse, while the pure wheat of faith that had been hidden in the prophetic stalk was stored away in the barns of the common master. This very name 'refuse' shows that the law is akin to it, and just as the seed could not have come into being without the refuse, so neither could the perfection of grace have been accomplished without the law.

Philippians 3:13: 'Forgetting what lies behind'—not as though those things were evil, but what Paul means is this: I do not occupy myself with remembering my past struggles, but with being anxious about what I will accomplish in what lies ahead.
Philippians 4:2: But some say that Euodia was the wife of the jailer, and Syntyche was the man.
